body.text: The basic investment tax credit rate is the 15% federal SR&ED ITC available to all claimants in Canada, including foreign-controlled subsidiaries, public corporations, individuals, partners and trust beneficiaries. It applies to qualified SR&ED expenditures of taxpayers ineligible for the 35% enhanced rate, and to CCPC and ECPC spending above the $6.0 million expenditure limit.

Between December 2024 and November 2026, Canada enacted the most expansive structural overhaul of its flagship Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program in decades. Following initial proposals in the December 16, 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES 2024) and draft legislation released on August 15, 2025, the federal government tabled Budget 2025 on November 4, 2025, and enacted Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Retroactive to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 doubled the annual SR&ED expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3.0 million (and the interim $4.5 million FES 2024 proposal) to $6.0 million, enabling qualifying corporations to claim up to $2.1 million annually in 100% refundable federal cash credits on current expenditures. Concurrently, the legislation expanded the prior-year taxable capital phase-out range from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, introduced an elective 3-year average gross revenue phase-out formula ($15 million–$75 million), extended the 35% enhanced refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), and restored both deduction and ITC eligibility for capital expenditures, shared-use equipment (SUE), and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024.

Further expanding this foundation, the CRA launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval regime on April 1, 2026—providing up-front technical eligibility determinations within eight weeks and halving post-filing expenditure review service standards from 180 days to 90 days—while Budget 2026 (tabled in November 2026) introduced a $930 million five-year ($235 million ongoing) SR&ED commercialisation expansion covering regulatory certification testing and intellectual property (IP) registration and maintenance costs for taxation years beginning on or after Budget Day. At the provincial level, Québec replaced eight legacy R&D tax measures with the unified, fully refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) (30% on the first $1.0 million above an exclusion threshold and 20% thereafter, including pre-commercialisation and capital equipment costs) for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025; British Columbia expressly harmonized with the federal $6.0 million limit, ECPC access, and capital expenditure restoration; Saskatchewan doubled its refundable CCPC threshold to $2.0 million and restored capital expenditure eligibility; and Ontario, Alberta, Manitoba, and the Atlantic provinces and Yukon maintained independent statutory caps and base definitions.
1. Statutory & Legislative Architecture of the Federal SR&ED Program
1.1 Dual-Mechanism Structure under the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations

Canada's federal SR&ED Tax Incentive Program operates through two distinct, complementary statutory mechanisms codified in the Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)) and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945). The first mechanism is the Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures governed by Section 37 of the Income Tax Act. Under subsection 37(1), a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada may pool allowable current and (for property acquired after December 15, 2024) capital SR&ED expenditures incurred in Canada that are related to a business of the taxpayer. Unlike ordinary business expenses under subsection 9(1), which must be deducted in the fiscal year incurred, the balance in the Section 37 expenditure pool may be deducted in full or in part in the current taxation year to reduce net income for tax purposes, or carried forward indefinitely as a running balance to offset business income in any subsequent taxation year.

The second statutory mechanism is the SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (ITC) governed by Sections 127 and 127.1 of the Income Tax Act. Under subsections 127(5) and 127(9), a claimant earns an ITC calculated as a specified percentage (15% basic rate or 35% enhanced rate) of its "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" at the end of the taxation year. Earned ITCs are first applied to reduce federal Part I tax otherwise payable under subsection 127(5); unused non-refundable ITCs may be carried back 3 taxation years or carried forward up to 20 taxation years. Where a claimant qualifies for cash refundability under section 127.1, the CRA refunds the designated percentage (40% or 100%) of the remaining current-year ITC balance directly to the taxpayer as a cash refund, which is statutorily deemed to have been deducted against Part I tax.

To prevent double-dipping between the two incentives, paragraph 37(1)(e) of the Income Tax Act mandates that any federal SR&ED ITC claimed to reduce Part I tax or refunded in cash in a given taxation year reduces the taxpayer's Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures in the immediately following taxation year. Conversely, provincial and territorial R&D tax credits (along with other government and non-government assistance) constitute "government assistance" under subsection 127(9), reducing both the Section 37 deductible pool (under paragraph 37(1)(d)) and the federal qualified expenditure pool for ITC purposes (under subsection 127(18)) in the same taxation year in which the provincial credit is earned, entitled to be received, or reasonably expected to be received.

body.text: 1.3 Subsection 248(1) Definition of SR&ED and the "Why" and "How" Framework

Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act defines scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis". This overarching preamble is followed by four inclusive paragraphs—paragraphs (a) through (d)—and seven explicit statutory exclusions—paragraphs (e) through (k).

Under the inclusive provisions, paragraph 248(1)(a) (Basic Research) covers work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view, while paragraph 248(1)(b) (Applied Research) covers work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. Paragraph 248(1)(c) (Experimental Development)—which accounts for the vast majority of commercial SR&ED claims in Canada—covers work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Finally, paragraph 248(1)(d) (Support Work) encompasses work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to only eight exhaustively enumerated activities—(i) engineering, (ii) design, (iii) operations research, (iv) mathematical analysis, (v) computer programming, (vi) data collection, (vii) testing, and (viii) psychological research—where the work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of work described in paragraph (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer. Support work cannot qualify as SR&ED on its own.

Conversely, paragraphs 248(1)(e) to (k) statutorily exclude seven categories of activity from SR&ED: (e) market research or sales promotion; (f) quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; (g) research in the social sciences or the humanities; (h) prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; (i) the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process; (j) style changes; and (k) routine data collection. Where an activity such as testing or data collection is performed routinely to support normal commercial operations, it is barred under paragraphs (f) and (k); however, when carried out specifically to test an experimental hypothesis and commensurate with the needs of experimental development under paragraph (c), it qualifies as eligible support work under paragraph (d).

On August 13, 2021, the CRA archived its former Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy and replaced it with the Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives. The current CRA guidelines operationalize subsection 248(1) and the Tax Court of Canada's jurisprudence into a two-pillar Why and How framework.

Under the "Why" Requirement (Scientific or Technological Uncertainty & Advancement), work must be conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement. The CRA distinguishes between generating conceptual knowledge (theories, explanatory relationships, or predictive models that advance the underlying technology base) and merely collecting factual knowledge (routine measurements or observations). New scientific or technological knowledge is needed only when there is an insufficiency or gap in the scientific or technological knowledge base—defined as the combined knowledge of internal business resources plus all publicly available knowledge reasonably accessible to competent professionals in the field. Typical indicators of technological uncertainty in experimental development include situations where existing design methods are inapplicable, system parameters operate outside normal ranges, interlocking constraints conflict, or too many interacting variables prevent predictable outcomes. If an uncertainty is circumvented via a standard workaround using existing knowledge, or resolved simply through on-the-job learning, employee training, hiring external experts, or purchasing off-the-shelf proprietary technology, the "Why" requirement is not met. Conversely, commercial or technical failure does not disqualify a project; demonstrating that a hypothesized technological approach cannot work eliminates an avenue of uncertainty and constitutes a valid technological advancement.

Under the "How" Requirement (Systematic Investigation or Search), the claimant must execute a structured scientific investigation comprising four sequential elements: (i) formulating a specific hypothesis (an idea or proposed causal relationship consistent with known facts that serves as a starting point for investigation); (ii) testing that hypothesis through controlled experiment or analysis; (iii) developing logical conclusions based on the analytical or experimental findings (which often lead to iterative hypothesis modification); and (iv) maintaining contemporaneous evidence generated as the work progresses.
1.4 Chronology of the 2024–2026 Legislative Reforms

Tax practitioners and corporate claimants auditing 2024, 2025, and 2026 taxation years must navigate three sequential federal legislative packages that progressively expanded the SR&ED program. In Phase 1 (The 2024 Fall Economic Statement of December 16, 2024 & Draft Legislation of August 15, 2025), the federal government proposed four major structural reforms effective for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (and for capital property acquired after December 15, 2024): increasing the annual expenditure limit for the 35% enhanced ITC from $3.0 million to $4.5 million; raising the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million; extending the 35% enhanced refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) using a 3-year average gross revenue phase-out ($15 million–$75 million), while allowing CCPCs to elect into the gross revenue phase-out structure; and restoring capital expenditure and lease cost eligibility for both the Section 37 deduction and ITCs. The Department of Finance released detailed draft legislative proposals for public consultation on August 15, 2025.

In Phase 2 (Budget 2025 of November 4, 2025 & Enactment of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026), Minister of Finance and National Revenue François-Philippe Champagne tabled the 2025 Federal Budget, which confirmed all FES 2024 measures and further increased the annual SR&ED expenditure limit from the proposed $4.5 million to $6.0 million, retroactively effective for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. These measures were enacted in Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Consequently, the $4.5 million limit was superseded prior to enactment, and $6.0 million is the legally enacted expenditure limit for all taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. Following Royal Assent, the CRA released updated Form T661 (Version 26) on May 15, 2026, updated Schedule T2SCH31 on May 22, 2026, updated Schedule T2SCH49 on May 29, 2026, and updated its core SR&ED policies between May and October 2026.

In Phase 3 (Budget 2026 Commercialisation and IP Expansion of November 2026), the federal government tabled a Notice of Ways and Means Motion committing $930 million over five years ($25 million in 2026–27, $200 million in 2027–28, $245 million in 2028–29, $225 million in 2029–30, and $235 million in 2030–31 and ongoing) to expand SR&ED eligibility to commercialisation activities for taxation years beginning on or after Budget Day. This expansion brings two previously excluded categories into the federal SR&ED base: (i) regulatory and certification testing, technological validations, and studies required for initial market approval of an SR&ED-developed product or process; and (ii) costs of preparing, filing, registering, and maintaining intellectual property protection (patents, certificates of supplementary protection, plant breeders' rights, and copyrighted software) arising from an eligible SR&ED project.
2. Federal Investment Tax Credit (ITC) Rates, Thresholds, Refundability & Carryovers
2.1 Basic (15%) and Enhanced (35%) ITC Rates

Under subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, the federal SR&ED program operates a two-tier ITC rate structure. The Basic ITC Rate (15%) is available to all claimants—including Canadian corporations (private or public), foreign-controlled subsidiaries carrying on business in Canada, individuals (sole proprietors), partners of a partnership, and beneficiaries of a trust. The 15% basic rate applies to all qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred by taxpayers ineligible for the enhanced rate, as well as to all qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred by CCPCs and ECPCs in excess of their annual expenditure limit.

The Enhanced ITC Rate (35%) consists of the 15% basic rate plus a 20% enhancement under subsection 127(10.1). For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the 35% rate was restricted exclusively to qualifying Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) up to a $3.0 million annual expenditure limit. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the 35% enhanced rate applies to both CCPCs and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) up to an annual expenditure limit of $6.0 million. When a claimant repays government assistance, non-government assistance, or a contract payment that previously reduced its qualified expenditures in an earlier taxation year, the ITC earned on the repayment is determined using the specified ITC rate (15% or 35%) at which the ITC would have been earned in the year the assistance or contract payment was originally received.
2.2 Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)

A centrepiece of the 2024–2026 reforms is the extension of the 35% enhanced refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. Previously, a Canadian technology or life-sciences company that completed an initial public offering (IPO) immediately lost its CCPC status, causing its SR&ED rate to drop from 35% refundable to 15% non-refundable.

To qualify as an ECPC throughout a taxation year, a corporation must satisfy three cumulative statutory conditions: (1) it must be resident in Canada throughout the taxation year; (2) it must have a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange (or have elected, or been designated by the Minister of National Revenue, to be a public corporation); and (3) it must not be controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons. Furthermore, Canadian-resident corporate subsidiaries in which all or substantially all (90% or more) of the issued shares are owned by one or more ECPCs are also eligible for the enhanced 35% refundable ITC regime.
2.3 Annual Expenditure Limit ($6.0 Million) and Dual Phase-Out Mechanics

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the maximum annual expenditure limit for both CCPCs (on an associated group basis) and ECPCs (on a consolidated corporate group basis) is $6,000,000. At the 35% enhanced rate, a $6,000,000 expenditure limit generates a maximum annual enhanced ITC of $2,100,000 (compared to $1,050,000 under the pre-December 16, 2024 $3.0 million limit, and $1,575,000 under the interim $4.5 million FES 2024 proposal).

The $6,000,000 expenditure limit is subject to a straight-line phase-out ("grind") between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000—a $60,000,000 phase-out corridor that replaces the pre-December 16, 2024 corridor of $10,000,000 to $50,000,000 (and historical qualifying income limit formulas such as $500,000 × [($40,000,000 − A) ÷ $40,000,000]). Under the Taxable Capital Method (Default for CCPCs), a CCPC's expenditure limit is reduced based on its taxable capital employed in Canada for the immediately preceding taxation year, combined across all associated CCPCs. Under the Gross Revenue Method (Mandatory for ECPCs; Elective for CCPCs under Subsection 127(10.32)), access to the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is phased out on a straight-line basis ($0.10 per dollar) when the corporation's average annual gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years is between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000. For an ECPC (or corporate group) that prepares consolidated financial statements, gross revenue is measured as reported in the group's annual financial statements at the highest level of consolidation presented to shareholders under GAAP (or standalone GAAP financial statements for standalone corporations), and all members of the consolidated group must share the $6,000,000 expenditure limit. Under subsection 127(10.32) of the Income Tax Act, a CCPC may elect (using a prescribed form) to have its expenditure limit determined under this 3-year average gross revenue structure instead of the taxable capital structure. Where a CCPC is associated with other CCPCs, all CCPCs in the associated group must jointly elect the revenue method, aggregating the revenues of all group members across the 3 preceding fiscal years (including shares of partnership or trust revenue, with reasonable adjustments allowed for intra-group sales). A dedicated schedule released in Fall 2026 governs the allocation of the expenditure limit under subsection 127(10.6) among associated CCPCs electing under subsection 127(10.32) or ECPCs in a consolidated group.
2.4 Refundability Matrix (Section 127.1 of the Income Tax Act)

A claimant with no federal Part I tax payable can receive part or all of its current-year earned ITC as a cash refund under section 127.1 of the Income Tax Act (which is statutorily deemed deducted against Part I tax) depending on its corporate classification, whether the ITC was earned at the 35% enhanced rate or the 15% basic rate, and whether the expenditure is current or capital.

For CCPCs and ECPCs that are Qualifying Corporations (and non-excluded), the CRA refunds 100% of the unclaimed balance of current-year ITCs earned at the 35% enhanced rate on qualified SR&ED expenditures of a current nature and the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) (up to $2.1 million annually on the $6.0 million limit). In addition, qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs receive a 40% cash refund on the unclaimed balance of current-year ITCs earned at the 35% enhanced rate on qualified SR&ED capital expenditures (an effective immediate cash refund of 35% × 40% = 14% of the capital cost), as well as a 40% cash refund on the unclaimed balance of ITCs earned at the 15% basic rate on qualified SR&ED expenditures exceeding the expenditure limit (an effective immediate cash refund of 15% × 40% = 6%).

For CCPCs that are NOT Qualifying Corporations (and non-excluded), the corporation still receives a 100% cash refund of unclaimed ITCs earned at the 35% enhanced rate on current expenditures and the PPA, and a 40% cash refund of unclaimed ITCs earned at the 35% enhanced rate on capital expenditures; however, any ITCs earned at the 15% basic rate by a non-qualifying CCPC are strictly non-refundable (0% refund). For other corporations (such as foreign-controlled subsidiaries or non-eligible public corporations), all ITCs are earned at the 15% basic rate and are strictly non-refundable. Finally, for individuals (sole proprietorships) and certain trusts, ITCs are earned at the 15% basic rate and are 40% refundable.
2.5 Carryback, Carryforward, and Pool Deductibility Rules

Under subsection 127(9), any portion of an earned SR&ED ITC that is not deducted against current-year Part I tax or refunded in cash under section 127.1 may be carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years to reduce prior federal Part I tax payable, or carried forward for up to 20 subsequent taxation years. By contrast, undeducted balances in the Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures never expire and may be carried forward indefinitely. Claiming a deduction from an already-established Section 37 pool in a future taxation year is not subject to the 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline in the year of deduction, provided the underlying expenditures were timely reported on Form T661 in the original year incurred.

If a corporation undergoes an acquisition of control (or a trust experiences a change in majority-interest beneficiary), a Loss Restriction Event (LRE) occurs under subsection 37(6.1) and paragraph 37(1)(h), triggering a deemed taxation year-end and reducing the Section 37 expenditure pool to nil. Undeducted balances in the pool prior to the LRE may be reinstated and deducted in a subsequent taxation year only if: (1) the business to which the SR&ED expenditures related continues to be carried on by the corporation for profit or with a reasonable expectation of profit; and (2) the deduction is claimed only to the extent of the corporation's income for the taxation year (before SR&ED deductions) derived from that same business or a similar business. Where a claimant is a partnership, paragraph 96(1)(e.1) prohibits carrying forward a Section 37 pool balance at the partnership level; the entire Section 37 pool must be deducted in full in computing the partnership's net income for the fiscal period in which the expenditures were incurred.

body.text: 3. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs), Calculation Methods, and Restoration of Capital & Lease Costs
3.1 Proxy Method vs. Traditional Method

Every taxation year, a claimant must elect on Part 3 of Form T661 to calculate its SR&ED expenditures using either the Proxy Method (Line 160, governed by clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) of the Income Tax Act and subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations) or the Traditional Method (Line 162, governed by clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) and subsections 2900(2) and 2900(3)). This election locks in on the day Form T661 is filed for the taxation year and cannot be changed for that taxation year.
A. The Proxy Method and the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA — 55%)

Under the Proxy Method, a claimant does not track, allocate, or claim actual SR&ED overhead and indirect supporting expenditures on Form T661 ($0 is entered on Line 360). Instead, in Part 5 of Form T661, the claimant computes a notional substitute amount—the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)—equal to 55% of the claimant's eligible salary base (a rate in effect since January 1, 2014, following reductions from 65% in 2012 and 60% in 2013).

Under subsection 127(9), the PPA (entered on Line 502 in Part 4 of Form T661) is included in "qualified expenditures" and therefore earns federal (and most provincial) SR&ED ITCs. However, the PPA is never added to the Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures. Instead, the actual underlying overhead expenses (utilities, office supplies, support staff wages, employer payroll taxes) remain deductible as ordinary business expenses under subsection 9(1) of the Income Tax Act. Only salaries and wages of employees directly engaged ("hands-on") in SR&ED in Canada (plus permissible foreign SR&ED wages) enter the Part 5 salary base. Under Regulation 2900(9), the following amounts are strictly excluded from the PPA salary base for all employees (whether specified employees or arm's length employees): taxable benefits under section 6, stock option benefits under section 7, bonuses, remuneration based on profits, prior-year unpaid salaries or wages paid in the current year (Line 310), and employer-paid related benefits.

To ensure that a corporation's notional PPA plus its other tax deductions cannot exceed its total actual business expenditures for the year, Regulation 2900(6) subjects the PPA to an overall ceiling calculated as:
PPA ≤ A − B − C

In this formula, A is the total amounts deducted in computing net income for tax purposes from the business for the year (including cost of goods sold); B is the sum of specific statutory deductions claimed in the year under Section 20 (e.g., Capital Cost Allowance, interest, bad debts), Section 24 (ceasing to carry on business), Section 26 (banks), Section 30 (land improvements for farming), Section 32 (insurance agents/brokers), Section 37 (the SR&ED deduction claimed on Line 411 of Schedule T2SCH1), Sections 66 to 66.8 (resource exploration and development), and Section 104 (trusts); and C is the total expenditures incurred in the year for the use of, or the right to use, a building (rent). If a claimant carries on more than one business, specified amounts deducted across all businesses must be summed.
B. The Traditional Method and the "Directly Attributable" Overhead Tests

Under the Traditional Method, the claimant forfeits the 55% PPA ($0 on Line 502) and instead claims actual SR&ED overhead and other expenditures on Line 360 of Form T661. These expenditures are added to both the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool and the qualified expenditure pool for ITCs.

Under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) of the Income Tax Act and paragraph 2900(2)(c) of the Income Tax Regulations, an overhead expenditure qualifies under the Traditional Method only if it is directly attributable to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada—which requires satisfying both the Directly Related Test and the Incremental Test. Under the Directly Related Test, the expenditure (or allocated portion thereof) must connect directly, without any intervening step or intermediary, to one of three elements: (1) the SR&ED work itself, (2) the SR&ED staff, or (3) the machinery or equipment used by staff to perform SR&ED. For example, non-technological clerical or administrative salaries aiding ongoing SR&ED, the employer's share of related benefits (CPP, EI, pension, medical/dental insurance), contractually mandated retiring allowances for hands-on SR&ED employees, moving expenses to relocate SR&ED employees within Canada, long-distance telephone charges, travel and lodging in Canada for testing at a customer location, training in Canada, incremental utilities, technical periodical subscriptions, waste disposal during active SR&ED, health and safety expenses, and fees paid to clinical study volunteers have a direct link and qualify. Conversely, related benefits, retiring allowances, training costs, or travel expenses for clerical or administrative staff who merely support SR&ED employees have an indirect link (an intervening step) and are disallowed.

Under the Incremental Test, the expenditure must be one that would not have been incurred had the prosecution of SR&ED not occurred. Fixed baseline costs (such as regular monthly telephone, cellular, or internet baseline charges, or fixed-cost maintenance contracts) fail the incremental test, whereas variable utility consumption (such as electricity varying in direct relation to the operating time of experimental equipment) passes the test. Additionally, under subsection 2900(3) of the Income Tax Regulations, the cost of maintenance and upkeep of premises, facilities, or equipment used for SR&ED is directly attributable without needing to separately prove the incremental test under paragraph 2900(2)(c).

Even if an expense is directly related and incremental, it is strictly barred if it is a prescribed expenditure under Section 2902 of the Income Tax Regulations: general administration or management of a business (subparagraph 2902(a)(i)), legal or accounting fees (clause 2902(a)(i)(B)), interest and financing costs under paragraphs 20(1)(c)–(g) (clause 2902(a)(i)(C)), entertainment expenses, advertising or selling expenses, convention or conference attendance fees (clause 2902(a)(i)(F)), scientific/technical society membership dues, fines or penalties, and fees paid to consultants or accountants to prepare the financial or technical SR&ED claim itself. Similarly, headhunter fees, job advertising, candidate interview travel, and immigration/work permit fees for hiring SR&ED personnel are deductible only as regular business expenses, whereas moving expenses to relocate selected SR&ED candidates or employees within Canada and taxable housing-loss benefits qualify under the Traditional Method.

body.text: To illustrate the numerical divergence between the two methods using the CRA's published policy benchmark, suppose a qualifying CCPC incurs $100,000 in directly engaged non-specified SR&ED salaries, $15,000 in consumed materials, and $50,000 in actual eligible SR&ED overhead. Under the Traditional Method, allowable SR&ED expenditures added to the Section 37 pool and qualified expenditures both equal $100,000 + $15,000 + $50,000 = $165,000, generating a 35% federal ITC of $57,750. Under the Proxy Method, allowable SR&ED expenditures added to the Section 37 pool equal $100,000 + $15,000 = $115,000 (while the $50,000 of actual overhead is deducted as an ordinary business expense), and the Part 5 PPA is $100,000 × 55% = $55,000, resulting in total qualified SR&ED expenditures of $115,000 + $55,000 = $170,000 and a 35% federal ITC of $59,500.
3.2 Salaries and Wages & Specified Employee Restrictions

Under the SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy (updated January 28, 2025), "salary or wages" takes its meaning from subsection 248(1) and sections 5 and 6 of the Income Tax Act, corresponding to gross employment income reported on an employee's T4 slip. Whether an employee is "directly engaged" in SR&ED is a question of fact based on the hands-on tasks performed (such as preparing equipment and materials for experiments, carrying out tests and analyses, collecting commensurate support data, or providing first-line direct technical supervision), rather than the employee's job title. For arm's length (non-specified) employees, claimable SR&ED wages (Line 300) include base salary, wages, overtime, regular earned vacation pay, statutory holiday pay, regular sick leave pay, pay in lieu of termination notice, bonuses, remuneration based on profits, inducements/non-competition payments for employment services, and cash outlays for taxable benefits (plus non-cash taxable benefits if the value is a reasonable estimate of actual cost, excludes recoverable GST/HST/PST, and the underlying cost is not deducted elsewhere as a business expense). Conversely, extended vacation or sick leave beyond normal annual earned entitlements, stock option benefits, retiring allowances, and employer shares of related benefits are excluded from SR&ED salary or wages.
A. Specified Employee Restrictions (Subsection 248(1) & Regulations 2900(7)–(8))

A specified employee of a claimant is an employee who does not deal at arm's length with the employer or is a specified shareholder (an individual who owns, directly or indirectly at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation). Because owner-managers control their own remuneration structure, the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations impose strict statutory caps on specified employees. First, no bonuses and no remuneration based on profits paid to a specified employee may be claimed as an SR&ED expenditure on Line 305. Second, the maximum SR&ED salary or wages that can be claimed on Line 305 of Form T661 for a specified employee is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the claimant's taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year that the individual is a specified employee:
Line 305 ceiling = 5 × YMPE × (number of days in the taxation year that the individual is a specified employee ÷ number of days in the taxation year)
For a taxation year ending in calendar year 2026, where the YMPE is $74,600, the maximum full-year Line 305 ceiling is $373,000 (5 × $74,600).

Third, under subsection 2900(7) of the Income Tax Regulations, the maximum amount of a specified employee's directly engaged SR&ED salary that may be included in the Part 5 salary base (Lines 852–858) to calculate the 55% PPA is restricted to the lesser of: (i) 75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages for the year (combining both SR&ED and non-SR&ED duties, and excluding bonuses, profit-based pay, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages); or (ii) 2.5 × YMPE, prorated by the total number of days in the taxation year that the claimant employed the individual (with no proration for the portion of the year during which the employee was not a specified employee):

Specified employee PPA salary base cap = the lesser of (75% × total salary or wages for the year) and (2.5 × YMPE × number of days in the taxation year that the individual was employed ÷ number of days in the taxation year)

For calendar year 2026 (YMPE = $74,600), the maximum full-year Part 5 PPA salary base cap per specified employee is $186,500 (2.5 × $74,600), which generates a maximum PPA of $186,500 × 55% = $102,575. If a specified employee is employed by two or more associated corporations in taxation years ending in the same calendar year, the 5 × YMPE and 2.5 × YMPE limits must be shared and formally allocated among the associated corporations using prescribed Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for SR&ED) under subsection 37(9.3) and Regulation 2900(8).
B. Unpaid Remuneration (180-Day Rule — Subsection 78(4)) and Foreign SR&ED Wages (10% Rule — Subsection 37(1.5))

Under subsection 78(4) of the Income Tax Act, any salary or wages incurred in a taxation year that are not paid within 180 days after the end of that taxation year are deemed not to have been incurred in that year. Such unpaid wages must be reported for tracking on Line 315 of Form T661 (excluded from current-year expenditures) and may only be claimed on Line 310 in the subsequent taxation year in which they are actually paid (though when paid in a subsequent year, they remain permanently excluded from the Part 5 PPA salary base under Regulation 2900(9)).

Under subsection 37(1.5), a claimant may include on Line 307 (non-specified employees) and Line 309 (specified employees) the salary or wages of employees performing SR&ED work outside Canada, up to a maximum combined ceiling of 10% of the total SR&ED salaries and wages directly attributable to SR&ED carried on in Canada (Lines 300 + 305). To qualify as "permissible salary or wages," all five statutory conditions must be met: (1) the SR&ED work is performed directly by an employee of the claimant and not a contractor; (2) the employee was a resident of Canada at the time the expense was incurred; (3) the work relates to a business of the claimant; (4) the work outside Canada is an integral part of, and solely in support of, an SR&ED project carried on in Canada; and (5) the remuneration paid is not subject to income or profits tax from another country.
3.3 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed, Prototypes, Pilot Plants, and Production Runs

Under the Materials for SR&ED Policy, "materials for SR&ED" must be physical, tangible raw materials, substances, or items (existing in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state) that at a given moment in the SR&ED process compose the body of a tangible object on which SR&ED is being carried out or that results from the SR&ED. Materials may be purchased from Canadian or foreign suppliers and are valued at their laid-down cost (invoice cost plus customs and excise duties, freight, transportation, and storage) or, for internally manufactured inventory, their industrial cost price (laid-down direct materials, direct labour, and properly chargeable production overhead), and may only be claimed in the taxation year in which they are actually consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada—never when merely purchased or moved into inventory.

Materials Consumed (Line 320) are materials destroyed or rendered virtually valueless as a direct result of the SR&ED. Under the CRA's 90% Rule, if 90% or more of a material's cost is consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED, 100% of its cost is allowable as materials consumed. Conversely, if experimental production is sold for more than 10% of its original cost, the input materials are not considered consumed. Materials Transformed (Line 325) are materials incorporated into a tangible object or altered during SR&ED that retain commercial or residual value. When a product or asset containing materials transformed is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use, the original cost of the materials transformed triggers ITC Recapture under subsections 127(27) to 127(36). General laboratory items that do not compose the body of the experimental object (such as petri dishes, beakers, flasks, pipettes, and test tubes), cleaning supplies, solvents, CDs/DVDs, off-the-shelf software licences or data purchases, used lubricants, general utilities (electricity, natural gas, oil), and utility or boiler feed water do not qualify as materials on Lines 320/325 (though incremental portions of lab supplies and utilities may be claimed as overhead on Line 360 if the Traditional Method is elected). Process water that physically enters an intermediate or final product in a chemical or industrial process and is rendered valueless qualifies as a material consumed.

Under the SR&ED while Developing an Asset Policy and SR&ED During Production Runs Policy, the CRA classifies physical assets developed during SR&ED into four distinct categories. First, a Prototype is an original trial model or preliminary version built to test the feasibility of a concept or hypothesis. Because a prototype usually has no lasting commercial value after testing, its design, construction, and testing labour and materials qualify as current expenditures (materials consumed). If a prototype retains value or multiple duplicate prototype copies are constructed for testing prior to commercial production and sold or retained, the input materials are claimed as materials transformed when testing is completed (not when constructed) and are subject to ITC recapture upon sale or commercial conversion. Second, a Pilot Plant is a non-commercial-scale production facility isolated from normal business operations and developed for the primary purpose of carrying out SR&ED over its useful life (with no intention of temporary or permanent conversion to commercial operations); current labour and materials to develop and operate a pilot plant qualify. Third, a Commercial Plant is any production facility intended for commercial use; claimants must strictly segregate incremental SR&ED labour and materials used to resolve technological uncertainties from commercial construction and excess production costs.

Fourth, for Custom Products / Commercial Assets, where a claimant develops a custom machine or commercial asset and it is impossible for either the claimant or the CRA to isolate the SR&ED work from the commercial construction work, the CRA permits an Alternative Approach:
Allowable SR&ED expenditures = (total actual cost of the project − estimated cost had the technology already existed) + cost of materials transformed in SR&ED

For example, if a custom machine project costs $150,000, would have cost an estimated $125,000 if the technology had already existed, and includes $30,000 of materials transformed in SR&ED, the allowable incremental SR&ED cost is $150,000 − $125,000 = $25,000, and total allowable SR&ED expenditures equal $25,000 + $30,000 = $55,000 (with the $30,000 of materials transformed subject to ITC recapture upon sale or commercial use). To use this Alternative Approach, three mandatory conditions must be met: (1) SR&ED work cannot be isolated by either the claimant or the CRA; (2) the CRA agrees to the use of the approach; and (3) the claimant agrees and signs a formal waiver of the right to object or appeal in respect of that issue under subsection 169(2.2) of the Income Tax Act.
3.4 Contract Expenditures and Third-Party Payments

When a claimant pays external parties in Canada to conduct SR&ED, the Income Tax Act distinguishes among arm's length SR&ED contracts, non-arm's length (NAL) SR&ED contracts, and third-party payments.

Where a claimant contracts an arm's length taxable supplier (Line 340) to perform SR&ED (basic research, applied research, experimental development, or commensurate paragraph (d) support work) in Canada on its behalf, 100% of the contract expenditure performed in the year is deductible in the Section 37 pool, while 80% of the expenditure enters the qualified expenditure pool to earn ITCs (a 20% statutory reduction applied in Part 4 of Form T661). Payments made for contracted SR&ED work not yet performed are excluded as prepaid expenses under subsection 18(9). To prevent duplication of ITCs, an arm's length contractor performing basic/applied research or experimental development must deduct the "contract payment" receivable from its own qualified expenditures (whereas an arm's length contractor performing only support work cannot claim SR&ED expenditures in its own right). Where SR&ED under a single contract is performed partially in Canada and partially outside Canada, the claimant must reasonably allocate the contract price; only the Canadian portion earns ITCs (at 80%), while the foreign portion may only be deducted against income under subsection 37(2).

Where a claimant enters into an SR&ED contract with a non-arm's length (NAL) performer (Line 345), 100% of the contract expenditure is an allowable deduction in the payer's Section 37 pool, but 0% qualifies for ITCs for the payer. Instead, the amount receivable by the NAL performer is not considered a contract payment under subsection 127(9), allowing the NAL performer to claim the SR&ED expenditures and ITCs directly. Alternatively, under subsection 127(13), the NAL performer may transfer all or a portion of its qualified SR&ED expenditures (including its PPA, up to the contract amount) to the payer (Line 508) by filing prescribed Form T1146 (Agreement to transfer qualified expenditures incurred in respect of SR&ED contracts between persons not dealing at arm's length). Under subsection 127(24), a claimant cannot circumvent NAL rules by interposing an arm's length party between itself and a NAL subcontractor if the main purpose is to obtain a qualified expenditure. Furthermore, when purchasing goods, materials, or capital property from a NAL supplier, subsection 127(11.6) limits the qualified expenditure for ITC purposes to the actual cost incurred by the NAL supplier, stripping any intercompany profit (Line 543 adjustment).

Under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1), (ii), and (iii), Third-Party Payments (Line 370 — Form T1263) are 100% deductible in the Section 37 pool and 80% eligible for ITCs when made to six designated categories of entities (Types A through F) for SR&ED carried on in Canada related to a business of the claimant, provided the claimant is entitled to exploit the results. Every third-party payment claimed on Line 370 requires attaching a completed Form T1263.

body.text: 3.5 Restored Eligibility of Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)

Between January 1, 2014, and December 15, 2024, capital expenditures, shared-use equipment, and equipment lease costs were completely excluded from the federal SR&ED program. Bill C-15 restored all three categories effective for property acquired (and available for use) or lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024.
A. All or Substantially All (ASA — ≥ 90%) Capital Expenditures (Paragraph 37(1)(b), Subsection 37(1.2), Line 390)

Under the updated SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026), an expenditure to acquire depreciable property after December 15, 2024 qualifies for both 100% immediate deduction in the Section 37 pool (Line 390) and SR&ED ITCs once it becomes available for use (under subsections 13(27) and 37(1.2)) if the claimant owns (or holds a leasehold interest in) the property and intends that it will either: (1) be used all or substantially all (90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada; or (2) have all or substantially all (90% or more) of its value consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada.

Land (non-depreciable), inventory, goodwill, buildings, and leasehold interests in buildings are statutorily excluded from Line 390 under paragraphs 37(8)(d) and (e). Furthermore, used depreciable property (equipment that was used in any manner prior to its SR&ED acquisition) qualifies for the 100% Section 37 income deduction on Line 390, but is a prescribed expenditure under Regulation 2902(b) that is ineligible for SR&ED ITCs (and must be deducted on Line 532 in Part 4 of Form T661)—unless a vendor refurbished the equipment so significantly prior to sale that it was restored to a "new" state of the art. If a claimant refurbishes its own used equipment after December 15, 2024, only the refurbishment costs qualify as an SR&ED capital expenditure for ITCs. In addition, because capital expenditures are once again eligible after December 15, 2024, the former subsection 37(14) "look-through rule" no longer reduces contract expenditures or third-party payments incurred after December 15, 2024 for non-current expenditures of the performer.
B. Shared-Use Equipment (SUE — Subsection 127(9), Line 504, Part 6C Boxes 788–796)

Under the updated SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (May 22, 2026), new depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024 that does not meet the 90% ASA threshold—because it is used for both SR&ED and commercial activities—qualifies as Shared-Use Equipment if its actual operating time in SR&ED in Canada is primarily (more than 50% but less than 90%). If actual SR&ED usage exceeds 50% of operating time during the "first period" (beginning when the property is acquired and available for use and ending at the end of the first taxation year that ends at least 12 months after that time), the asset qualifies as First-Term SUE and 25% (1/4) of its capital cost (excluding borrowed money costs under section 21) is deemed a qualified expenditure on Line 504. If the asset qualified as First-Term SUE and its actual SR&ED usage exceeds 50% of operating time during the "second period" (from acquisition to the end of the first taxation year ending at least 24 months after acquisition), it qualifies as Second-Term SUE, earning an additional 25% (1/4) of its capital cost (cumulatively 50% across both periods) on Line 504.

The capital cost of SUE is not added to the Section 37 deductible pool; instead, the claimant depreciates the equipment under regular Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) rules on Schedule T2SCH8, and any SUE ITC applied or refunded reduces the undepreciated capital cost (UCC) of the CCA class in the subsequent taxation year. SUE excludes used property, General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF), and Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under Regulation 2900(11)—which disallows property intended at the time of acquisition to be used during the assembly, construction, or commissioning of a commercial manufacturing facility, plant, or line (paragraph 2900(11)(c)) or intended to be used primarily for non-SR&ED purposes over its expected useful life (paragraph 2900(11)(d)).
C. Equipment Lease Costs and Computer Hardware/Software Rules (Lines 350, 355 & 360; Box 759)

Under the updated SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8, 2026), lease expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024 for equipment used in SR&ED in Canada qualify depending on the calculation method and operating time percentage (for tax years straddling December 16, 2024, SR&ED operating time is measured over the period after December 15, 2024). Where leased equipment is used ASA (90% or more) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada, 100% of the lease expenditure is claimed on Line 350 under both the Proxy Method (excluding GPOEF) and the Traditional Method (including GPOEF). Where leased equipment is used primarily (more than 50% but less than 90%) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada, a claimant using the Proxy Method claims 50% (half) of the lease cost (excluding GPOEF) on Line 355 (and 0% if usage is 50% or less). Under the Traditional Method, $0 is entered on Line 355, and for any SR&ED usage under 90%, the exact proportional percentage of the lease cost (including GPOEF or land leases) may be claimed on Line 360 as overhead and other expenditures if directly related and incremental to SR&ED.

Crucially, the CRA's SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy defines GPOEF as furniture (desks, chairs, lamps, filing cabinets, bookshelves), photocopiers, fax machines, telephones, cell phones, and calculators, and explicitly confirms that computers (including computer hardware, software, and ancillary equipment) are NOT considered GPOEF. Consequently, lease payments for computer hardware, software, and ancillary systems incurred after December 15, 2024 qualify for SR&ED lease claims under both the Proxy and Traditional methods. Outlays for the use or right to use a building (rent) remain strictly excluded under both methods, except for lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024 for a prescribed special-purpose building approved by the Department of Finance Canada under Regulation 2903.
3.6 Unpaid Amounts, Government Assistance, and ITC Recapture

Under subsection 127(26) of the Income Tax Act, current SR&ED expenditures other than salary or wages (such as materials, arm's length contracts, overhead, and lease costs) that are not paid within 180 days after the end of the taxation year must be deducted from qualified expenditures on Line 520 of Form T661 in the year incurred. An unpaid expenditure must be identified on Form T661 on or before the 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline for the year incurred; if omitted, it can never be included in qualified expenditures even when paid. When a timely identified unpaid expenditure is paid in a subsequent year, it is added back on Line 500 (at 80% of the amount paid if it was an arm's length SR&ED contract).

Under the Assistance and Contract Payments Policy (updated March 27, 2026), any government assistance, non-government assistance, or contract payment that a claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before its filing-due date reduces both the Section 37 pool and qualified expenditures (Lines 513 to 518) on a project-by-project basis. Assistance for one project cannot reduce the expenditures of an unrelated project unless transferred within a non-arm's length group via Form T1145 under subsection 127(20) (Line 540). If an agreement provides funding whose repayment depends conditionally on future revenues or royalties, the CRA treats the funding as a forgivable loan constituting government assistance.

Under subsections 127(27) to 127(36), if a claimant claims an SR&ED ITC on property—specifically (1) materials transformed, (2) ASA capital equipment acquired after December 15, 2024, (3) Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) acquired after December 15, 2024, or (4) physical property (other than intellectual property) acquired through an arm's length SR&ED contract—and subsequently sells the property or converts it to commercial use, ITC Recapture applies. The recaptured ITC—calculated as the lesser of the ITC originally earned on the property and the applicable historical ITC rate applied to the proceeds of disposition (or fair market value upon conversion to commercial use)—is added directly to federal Part I tax payable in the year of disposition or conversion, while simultaneously increasing the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool in the following taxation year under paragraph 37(1)(c.2). If a component part is ordered from an arm's length supplier for $12,000, the entire $12,000 cost is subject to recapture; if the same component is manufactured in-house, recapture applies only to the cost of the materials transformed, and never to the in-house salaries or overhead.
3.7 Budget 2026 Commercialisation & Intellectual Property Protection Expansion

For taxation years beginning on or after Budget Day 2026, the federal $930 million commercialisation expansion adds two major categories to the SR&ED program. First, under Regulatory and Certification Requirements, eligible SR&ED activities are expanded to include tests, technological validations, and studies conducted to meet regulatory requirements necessary to obtain the initial approval or certification required to commercialise a product or process, provided the activities directly relate to an eligible SR&ED project. All expenditure types eligible under the standard SR&ED program (wages and salaries, materials, contracting costs, overhead, and machinery and equipment) can be claimed for these regulatory activities.

Second, under Intellectual Property (IP) Protection, eligible SR&ED expenditures are expanded to include costs reasonably incurred to prepare, file, obtain (register), and periodically maintain legal protection for IP developed in the course of conducting an eligible SR&ED project. Eligible forms of IP protection encompass patents, certificates of supplementary protection, plant breeders' rights, and copyrighted software registered or protected under relevant Canadian legislation or equivalent legislation in another jurisdiction. While official administrative fees payable to an IP office outside Canada qualify, costs of supporting activities (such as preparing and drafting an application) are eligible only if those supporting activities are conducted in Canada. Costs incurred to enforce IP rights (such as patent infringement litigation) are excluded, and if a taxpayer subsequently disposes of IP for which SR&ED IP-protection support was claimed, recapture rules apply to recover both the related SR&ED deduction and the ITC.
4. Governing Bodies, Pre-Claim Approval, Filing Deadlines, Prescribed Forms & Review Procedures
4.1 Governing Authorities

The federal SR&ED program is administered by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) through its Business Tax Incentives Directorate and regional SR&ED Coordinating Tax Services Offices (CTSOs), which deploy dual-specialist audit teams consisting of a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) (evaluating scientific and technological eligibility under subsection 248(1) and reporting to a Research and Technology Manager [RTM]) and a Financial Reviewer (FR) (auditing expenditure calculations, salary caps, overhead allocations, and ITC schedules and reporting to a Financial Review Manager [FRM]). The CRA also administers all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits through the unified T2 corporate income tax system, with only two exceptions: Québec (where the CRA performs the scientific review of R&D activities while Revenu Québec and the Ministère de l'Économie, de l'Innovation et de l'Énergie administer the CRIC on provincial Form RD-1029.8.CR-T) and Alberta (where Alberta Treasury Board and Finance independently administers the Innovation Employment Grant). Tax policy and legislative design rest with the Department of Finance Canada, while Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED), the National Research Council of Canada (NRC) (including NRC-IRAP), the Canadian Intellectual Property Office (CIPO), and the federal granting councils (NSERC, SSHRC, and CIHR) administer complementary federal innovation grants and IP frameworks.
4.2 Optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026)

On April 1, 2026, pursuant to the Canada Strong Budget 2025 initiative, the CRA launched a formal, optional Pre-Claim Approval process inside the SR&ED Client Portal in My Business Account. This process enables eligible businesses to have their planned work evaluated by the CRA to confirm that it meets SR&ED technical eligibility requirements before beginning work or incurring substantial costs.

To qualify for pre-claim approval, the business must be a CCPC, other Canadian corporation, or Canadian partnership, have annual gross business income of less than $25 million, and be in good standing with the CRA. The submitted project (up to a maximum of 3 projects per application) must not have been included in a previous SR&ED claim and must not involve issues currently under litigation. Eligible businesses apply through four sequential steps:

items: Request a Case Number: Complete a web form (taking less than five minutes) to confirm eligibility; the CRA issues a pre-claim approval case number within 2 to 5 business days.

Complete and Submit the Application in My Business Account: Enter business identification details (Lines 010–016), project title, anticipated project start date, estimated total SR&ED expenditures, field of science or technology code from Appendix 1 of Guide T4088 (Lines 020–026), technical contact person (Lines 028–032), and two structured technical narratives—Line 042 (What scientific or technological uncertainty do you aim to address? — maximum 500 words) and Line 043 (What due diligence have you completed to confirm that the scientific or technical uncertainty described in line 042 cannot be resolved using existing knowledge, solutions or approaches? — maximum 700 words)—and upload up to 10 supporting documents under "Submit documents" in My Business Account.

Meet with a CRA Research and Technology Advisor (Within 4 Weeks): Within four weeks of submitting the completed application, an assigned RTA conducts a 2-to-5-hour virtual or on-site meeting (mandatory for new SR&ED claimants and claimants not in good standing; optional at the RTA's discretion for existing claimants in good standing) to discuss the state of technology, the scientific or technological uncertainty, the initial hypothesis, and planned experiments.

Receive Written Pre-Claim Approval Determination (Within 8 Weeks): Within eight weeks of completing the application in My Business Account, the CRA issues a formal Pre-Claim Approval Evaluation Report confirming whether pre-claim approval is granted.

Whether or not pre-claim approval is obtained, the claimant must still submit Form T661 after the end of the taxation year (ticking Line 212 and entering the pre-claim approval case number on Line 214). For refundable SR&ED claims containing only pre-claim-approved projects that are selected for an expenditure-only review, the CRA's processing service standard is cut in half from 180 calendar days to 90 calendar days. There is no formal objection process if pre-claim approval is not granted; the business may either modify its application with a new case number or proceed to file a standard post-year-end SR&ED claim.
4.3 Statutory Filing Deadlines and the Subsection 220(2.2) Non-Waiver Bar

Under subsection 37(11) and paragraph (m) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, a taxpayer's SR&ED reporting deadline is strictly 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year in which the expenditures were incurred. Because a corporation's T2 income tax return filing-due date is 6 months after the end of its taxation year, a corporation's statutory SR&ED reporting deadline is 18 months after the end of its taxation year (if a tax year ends on the last day of a month, such as February 28, the T2 due date is August 31 and the SR&ED reporting deadline is August 31 of the following year; if the tax year ends mid-month, such as January 6, the SR&ED deadline falls on July 6 of the following year). For an individual (Form T1, due June 15), the SR&ED reporting deadline is June 15 of the second following calendar year (17.5 months after a December 31 year-end); for a trust (Form T3, due 90 days after year-end), the deadline is 15 months after its taxation year-end.

Under subsection 37(11.1) and paragraph 127(9)(m), if a claimant fails to file prescribed Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 (or Form T2038(IND)) containing the prescribed information for each expenditure and project on or before the SR&ED reporting deadline, the unclaimed or late-filed expenditures are statutorily deemed not to be SR&ED expenditures and zero ITC is earned. Furthermore, pursuant to subsection 220(2.2) of the Income Tax Act (in force since November 17, 2005), a taxpayer cannot request a ministerial waiver or extension under subsection 220(2.1) in respect of prescribed forms or prescribed information specified for SR&ED tax incentives. The 18-month deadline is absolute and non-extendable.

body.text: 4.5 CRA Review Process, Service Standards, Administrative Review (Form RC532), and Gross Negligence Penalties
A. Processing Service Standards and the Three-Step Review Workflow

Once a complete SR&ED claim and income tax return are received, the CRA operates under three published service standards for refundable claims (there are no service standards for non-refundable claims): 60 calendar days for refundable claims accepted as filed without review; 90 calendar days for refundable claims selected for an expenditure-only review where all claimed projects were granted Pre-Claim Approval; and 180 calendar days (90% compliance target) for refundable claims selected for a full technical and financial review (including claims containing unapproved projects or projects that materially differed from their Pre-Claim Approval). First-time claimants (or claimants who have not filed an SR&ED claim in the preceding three years) may be selected for the mandatory First-Time Claimant Advisory Service (FTCAS), which provides recommendations and guidance to support future claims. Under The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants (updated July 2, 2025 and April 20, 2026), a standard technical and financial review follows three sequential steps:

items: Step 1 — The Start of the Review: A reviewer contacts the claimant by telephone to notify them of the review, introduce the assigned RTA and FR, confirm official language preference, identify the specific projects and financial issues under review, establish secure communication methods, and schedule a virtual (or on-site) review meeting.

Step 2 — The Review Meeting and Requests for Additional Information: Reviewers interview R&D staff, project managers, and financial personnel, conduct a virtual or physical tour of the facility/premises, examine contemporaneous supporting evidence for the work (dated documents, photos, logs, scrap/artifacts) and accounting records (ledgers, journals, receipts, contracts, vouchers), verbally share preliminary review findings, and issue follow-up requests for any missing information with clear deadlines.

Step 3 — The End of the Review and Proposal Package: The RTA prepares an SR&ED Project Eligibility Report, which the FR uses to adjust allowable and qualified expenditures. If adjustments are proposed, the CRA sends a Proposal Package containing the SR&ED Project Eligibility Report, a proposal letter summarizing the proposed adjustments to expenditures, ITCs, and any proposed penalties, and financial working papers, granting the claimant 30 calendar days to submit written representations before a Notice of Assessment or Reassessment is issued.

body.text: B. Four-Tier Dispute Escalation Hierarchy and Form RC532 Administrative Review
Under the Guidelines for resolving claimants' SR&ED concerns (updated December 5, 2025), a claimant disputing an RTA's or FR's findings must escalate through four sequential steps:

items: Step 1 — Talk with the Reviewer(s): Address technical or financial misunderstandings directly with the assigned RTA and/or FR as early as possible.
Step 2 — Contact the Reviewer's Manager(s): Escalate unresolved concerns to the Research and Technology Manager (RTM) and/or Financial Review Manager (FRM).

Step 3 — Request an Administrative Review (Form RC532): After receiving the Proposal Package—and before the expiry of the 30-day proposal period and before the file is closed—the claimant may submit Form RC532 (Administrative Review Form) to the National SR&ED Administrative Review Intake Centre (Canada Revenue Agency, Business Tax Incentives Directorate, Enterprise Building, 13th Floor, 427 Laurier Ave W, Ottawa ON K1A 0L5). Forwarded within 3 business days to the local SR&ED Assistant Director, the Administrative Review is not a second technical review; rather, the Assistant Director determines whether (i) the claimant was given due process (reasonable opportunity and time to explain the work, clear requests for clarification, consideration of all submitted evidence, clear explanations in the report and proposal package, and reasonable time to respond) and (ii) the technical and financial reviews were consistent with current SR&ED legislation, policies, and procedures.

Step 4 — Formal Notice of Objection and Tax Court of Canada Appeal: Once the final assessment or reassessment is issued, a claimant that still disagrees may file a formal Notice of Objection with the CRA Appeals Branch within 90 days of the date of the Notice of Assessment or Reassessment, and subsequently appeal to the Tax Court of Canada.

body.text: C. Gross Negligence Penalties on Overstated SR&ED Claims (Subsection 163(2))

Under the Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy (updated January 28, 2025), where a claimant knowingly, or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence, makes, participates in, agrees to, or accepts a false statement or omission in an initial or amended SR&ED claim, subsection 163(2) of the Income Tax Act imposes a civil penalty. Under subsection 163(3), the CRA bears the burden of establishing on a balance of probabilities (more likely than not) that the false statement or omission resulted from intentional conduct or gross negligence rather than a simple oversight or misunderstanding of the Act—such as including projects the claimant knew did not involve SR&ED, fabricating SR&ED activities that never occurred, claiming personal expenses or false invoices, or continuing to claim non-qualifying, miscalculated, or unsubstantiated amounts after being advised in writing by the CRA.

Furthermore, there is no concept of a "withdrawn" SR&ED claim in the Income Tax Act: once an income tax return containing an SR&ED claim is filed and selected for review, a request to withdraw the claim is legally treated as an amended return reducing the claim, which does not stop the audit and does not prevent the application of subsection 163(2) penalties based on the original return (nor is the Voluntary Disclosures Program available once a review has commenced).
When the CRA meets its burden of proof under subsection 163(3), the gross negligence penalty is calculated as:
Penalty = the greater of $100 and 50% × (understated Part I tax + overstated refundable ITC claimed)

In applying this formula, if a disallowed SR&ED expenditure still constitutes a valid ordinary business expenditure, net income is not understated; however, if the disallowed item is a personal expense or false invoice, it creates an understatement of income under subsection 163(2.1) (even in a net loss year, where taxable income is deemed not to be less than zero and theoretical Part I tax is calculated). Under the CRA's ordering rules, overstated expenditures in the Section 37 pool and overstated ITCs are deemed to be deducted first before any legitimate pool balances or legitimate opening, transferred, or current-year ITCs. If a claimant requests additional discretionary deductions (such as additional Capital Cost Allowance) during the review to offset disallowed expenditures, the CRA accepts the CCA deduction for tax assessment purposes but ignores the additional deduction when calculating the understated Part I tax for the penalty. Crucially, when gross negligence applies to the refund of an overstated refundable ITC under paragraph 163(2)(d), the CRA calculates the 50% penalty on the entire overstated refundable ITC claimed, regardless of whether a portion of that overstated refund resulted from a simple oversight.
