body.text: 5.2 Detailed Jurisdiction-by-Jurisdiction Technical Analysis
A. Québec — The 2025–2026 CRIC Overhaul (Form RD-1029.8.CR-T)

In the 2025–2026 Québec Budget tabled on March 25, 2025, Finance Minister Éric Girard enacted a sweeping structural consolidation of Québec's R&D tax system. Effective for taxation years (or partnership fiscal periods) beginning after March 25, 2025, Québec introduced the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (Crédit d'impôt pour la recherche, l'innovation et la commercialisation — CRIC) and simultaneously abolished eight legacy Québec R&D tax measures: (1) the Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D) (formerly Form RD-1029.7, which offered 14% to 30% rates phased out between $50M and $75M of assets); (2) the Tax Credit for University Research or Research Carried Out by a Public Research Centre or a Research Consortium (formerly Form RD-1029.8.6); (3) the Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium (with transitional rules permitting existing eligible fee balances at the end of a tax year ending after March 25, 2025 to be claimed for taxation years ending on or before December 31, 2029); (4) the Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research; (5) the Tax Credit for Technological Adaptation Services; (6) the Industrial Design Component of the in-house design tax credits (effective for taxation years beginning after December 31, 2025, while the fashion design component remains unchanged); (7) the Tax Holiday for Foreign Researchers and Experts; and (8) related legacy R&D measures.

Under the CRIC regime (Form RD-1029.8.CR-T), any corporation (or corporate member of a partnership) that operates a business in Québec and maintains an establishment there qualifies for a 100% refundable tax credit—regardless of corporate asset size—at a rate of 30% on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures exceeding the applicable exclusion threshold (shared among associated corporations), and 20% on all qualified expenditures exceeding that $1,000,000 limit. For each taxation year, a corporation's qualified expenditures must exceed an exclusion threshold equal to the greater of: (1) $50,000; or (2) the sum, across all employees engaged in eligible R&D and pre-commercialisation activities, of the basic personal amount of the applicable Québec personal income tax system for each employee, adjusted to reflect the proportion of time spent by the employee on eligible R&D or pre-commercialisation activities.

While Québec's definition of R&D (basic research, applied research, and experimental development) is harmonized with federal legislation and the CRA carries out the scientific review of R&D work, the CRIC also covers pre-commercialisation activities undertaken in conjunction with (and as a continuation of) R&D work carried out in Québec by the corporation or on its behalf. Eligible pre-commercialisation activities include: (i) tests, technological validations, and studies carried out to meet regulatory requirements aimed at obtaining an initial approval or certification for the purpose of commercialising an innovation (including quality control activities strictly related to implementing a quality control system required to obtain initial approval or certification); and (ii) product design, including developing form and aesthetics, improving functionality, and selecting materials. CRIC qualified expenditures consist of 100% of salaries and wages paid to the corporation's employees in Québec, 50% of amounts paid to a subcontractor for a contract carried out in Québec, 50% of payments made to an eligible public research centre, eligible research consortium, or eligible university entity, and 100% of property acquisition costs (capital equipment), excluding land, buildings, or rights to use land or buildings. A corporation cannot claim both the CRIC and another Québec tax credit (such as the C3i investment and innovation credit or the Large Investment Project tax holiday) for the same property expenditure.
B. Ontario — Tri-Credit Ecosystem (Schedules 566, 508, 568 & 569)

Ontario operates three distinct corporate R&D tax credits under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), all administered by the CRA and requiring a permanent establishment in Ontario plus a timely filed federal Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31. First, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Schedule 566, Section 96) provides an 8% fully refundable credit to CCPCs on up to $3,000,000 of qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures (maximum annual refund of $240,000, entered on Line 468 of Schedule 5). Unlike the federal government and British Columbia, Ontario did not adopt the $6.0 million expenditure limit, ECPC access, or the $15M–$75M phase-out range. Instead, the OITC remains capped at $3.0 million (shared among associated corporations), includes 100% of qualifying current expenditures (without confirming inclusion of restored federal capital expenditures), and phases out when the associated group's prior-year federal taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000 or prior-year specified capital is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000. A corporation may waive all or part of its OITC under subsection 96(14).

Second, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Schedule 508) provides a 3.5% non-refundable credit on qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures to all corporations (entered on Line 416 of Schedule 5) with no expenditure limit. Unused ORDTC balances carry back 3 years and forward 20 years.

Third, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC — Schedules 568 & 569, Section 97) provides a 20% fully refundable tax credit (entered on Line 470 of Schedule 5) on qualified current monetary expenditures (excluding payments in kind) incurred under an eligible contract with an Eligible Research Institute (ERI) in Ontario—including Ontario universities, colleges of applied arts and technology, hospital research institutes, Ontario Centres of Excellence, and federal Networks of Centres of Excellence. The corporation must not be "connected" to the ERI (defined as the ERI owning more than 10% of voting rights or more than 10% of the fair market value of all issued shares, or not dealing at arm's length). Qualified expenditures are capped at $20,000,000 annually across an associated group (allocated under subsection 38(4) of Ontario Regulation 37/09), yielding up to $4,000,000 in cash refunds per year. A single eligible contract with an Ontario research institute can simultaneously qualify for the 20% OBRITC, the 8% OITC, the 3.5% ORDTC, and the federal SR&ED ITC.
C. Western, Prairie, Atlantic, and Northern Regimes

British Columbia (Form T666 / Schedule 425) enacted express alignment with the 2024–2026 federal Bill C-15 reforms. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, B.C. doubled its 10% refundable SR&ED expenditure limit from $3.0 million to $6.0 million (increasing the maximum annual cash refund from $300,000 to $600,000), extended the 10% refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), raised its prior-year taxable capital phase-out range to $15 million–$75 million, restored capital expenditures to the B.C. qualifying base, and in B.C. Budget 2026 removed the credit's former September 1, 2027 expiry date to make the program permanent. Expenditures above the $6.0 million limit (or by other corporations) earn a 10% non-refundable credit (3-year carryback, 10-year carryforward), which can be renounced.

Alberta (Innovation Employment Grant — AB Schedule 9 / Schedule 16) eliminated its former 10% SR&ED tax credit for work performed after January 1, 2020, and introduced the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) for eligible expenditures incurred after December 31, 2020 under sections 26.95 to 26.99 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act. Administered by Alberta Treasury Board and Finance with a filing deadline of 15 months after the corporation's filing-due date, the IEG provides a fully refundable payment equal to 8% of eligible Alberta R&D spending up to the corporation's base spending level (its average eligible R&D spending over the preceding two years) plus an additional 12% incremental benefit (20% combined rate) on eligible spending exceeding that 2-year base, up to a maximum annual expenditure cap of $4,000,000. On June 30, 2026, Alberta published updated technical guidance confirming that its existing IEG framework and $4.0 million cap continue to apply without adopting the federal $6.0 million limit.

Saskatchewan (Schedule 403) enhanced its 10% R&D tax credit in the March 18, 2026 Saskatchewan Budget (effective for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024) by: (1) doubling the annual qualifying expenditure limit on which a CCPC can claim a 10% refundable credit from $1.0 million to $2.0 million (increasing the maximum annual cash refund from $100,000 to $200,000); and (2) restoring eligibility for capital expenditures (new machinery and equipment) and related lease/rental costs for both the refundable and non-refundable credits. Qualifying expenditures exceeding $2.0 million (and expenditures by non-CCPCs) earn a 10% non-refundable credit (3-year carryback, 10-year carryforward, renounceable), subject to an overall cap of $1,000,000 in total combined refundable and non-refundable credits annually.

Manitoba (Schedule 380) provides a 15% R&D tax credit with no expenditure limit. Where eligible R&D is conducted under contract with a qualifying Manitoba research institute, the entire 15% credit is 100% refundable; for in-house R&D, 50% (7.5% rate) is refundable and 50% (7.5% rate) is non-refundable (3-year carryback, 20-year carryforward). Manitoba already recognized capital expenditures on depreciable property (excluding buildings and leasehold interests in buildings) prior to the federal restoration. For federal SR&ED purposes, a corporation must renounce the Manitoba credit on or before 6 months after its taxation year-end.

Nova Scotia (Schedule 340), New Brunswick (Schedule 360), Newfoundland and Labrador (Schedule 301 / Form T1129), and Yukon (Schedule 442) all provide a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit with no annual expenditure cap. Yukon provides an additional 5% refundable credit (20% total) on eligible amounts paid or payable to Yukon University. Newfoundland and Labrador uniquely provides that eligible expenditures for the 15% NL credit are not reduced by government or non-government assistance (except GST/HST input tax credits). Nova Scotia permits full renouncement of current-year credits under subsection 41(7) of the Income Tax Act (Nova Scotia) on or before the T2 filing-due date (6 months after year-end), and both Nova Scotia and New Brunswick apply property recapture rules.
5.3 Mathematical Modelling of the Federal-Provincial Assistance "Grind"

Because subsection 127(18) and paragraph 37(1)(d) of the Income Tax Act classify provincial and territorial R&D tax credits as government assistance, provincial credits reduce the federal qualified expenditure pool dollar-for-dollar in the year earned. Consequently, the combined federal-provincial credit rate is never simple addition; for a provincial credit rate p and a federal ITC rate f applied to the identical expenditure base, the effective combined credit rate on qualified expenditures is:
Combined rate = p + f × (1 − p)

In Case Study 1A (Ontario CCPC with $500,000 Direct Salaries under the Proxy Method), a CCPC incurring $500,000 in direct hands-on SR&ED salaries in Ontario (Line 300) adds a 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount of $275,000 (Line 502) for a pre-assistance qualified expenditure base of $775,000. Assuming the CCPC claims the 8% refundable OITC on Schedule 566 (and waives the 3.5% non-refundable ORDTC), it earns $62,000 ($775,000 × 8%), which reduces the federal qualified expenditure base on Line 513 to $713,000 ($775,000 − $62,000). The 35% federal enhanced ITC on $713,000 yields $249,550, resulting in a total cash refund of $311,550—an effective refundable rate of 40.20% of total qualified expenditures (8% + 35% × 92%), or 62.31% of direct cash salary outlay ($311,550 ÷ $500,000). (If the CCPC also claims the 3.5% non-refundable ORDTC of $27,125, total provincial assistance is $89,125 [11.5%], reducing the federal base to $685,875 and yielding a 35% federal refund of $240,056.25 plus $62,000 OITC cash plus $27,125 ORDTC tax offset = $329,181.25, or 65.84% of direct salary.)

In Case Study 1B (Ontario CCPC with $6,000,000 Qualified Expenditures — Post-Bill C-15 Cap Divergence), the federal expenditure limit is $6,000,000 while Ontario's OITC remains capped at $3,000,000. On the first $3,000,000 band, the CCPC earns the maximum 8% OITC of $240,000, grinding the federal base on that band to $2,760,000 and generating a 35% federal ITC of $966,000 (subtotal of $1,206,000, or 40.20%). On the second $3,000,000 band ($3.0M to $6.0M), the OITC is $0 (no provincial grind), so the CCPC earns the full unground 35% federal ITC of $1,050,000 ($3,000,000 × 35%), producing a combined cash refund of $2,256,000 (a blended cash rate of 37.60% on $6.0 million).

In Case Study 2 (Québec Corporation under the Post-March 25, 2025 CRIC with $1,000,000 Direct Salaries), suppose 10 full-time R&D engineers in Québec earn $100,000 each ($1,000,000 total direct wages) and the corporation's employee-based CRIC exclusion threshold is $180,000 (10 × $18,000 basic personal amount, exceeding the $50,000 floor). The corporation claims the 30% refundable CRIC on $820,000 ($1,000,000 − $180,000) on Form RD-1029.8.CR-T, earning $246,000. Federally, under the Proxy Method, pre-assistance qualified expenditures equal $1,000,000 (wages) + $550,000 (55% PPA) = $1,550,000, which is reduced by the $246,000 CRIC on Line 513 to $1,304,000. At the 35% enhanced rate, the federal refundable ITC is $456,400 ($1,304,000 × 35%), yielding a combined cash refund of $702,400 ($246,000 + $456,400), or 70.24% of direct cash salary outlay.

In Case Study 3 (British Columbia CCPC or ECPC with $6,000,000 Qualified Expenditures), because B.C. expressly aligned its Form T666 regime with Bill C-15, a qualifying CCPC or ECPC incurring $6,000,000 in qualified B.C. SR&ED expenditures earns the full 10% B.C. refundable credit of $600,000. This grinds the federal qualified expenditure base to $5,400,000 ($6,000,000 − $600,000), generating a 35% federal refundable ITC of $1,890,000 and a total combined cash refund of $2,490,000 (41.50% of total qualified expenditures, or 64.325% of direct salaries when the base consists of salaries plus the 55% PPA).

body.text: 6. Judicial Precedents & Tax Court / Federal Court of Appeal Jurisprudence
6.1 The Foundational Five-Question Test: Northwest Hydraulic, RIS-Christie, and C.W. Agencies

Canadian SR&ED jurisprudence is anchored by three foundational decisions that remain binding law across the Tax Court of Canada and the Federal Court of Appeal. In Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 DTC 1839, 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC), Justice Donald Bowman (as he then was) articulated the governing judicial approach to experimental development at paragraphs 14 to 16. Justice Bowman established that technological risk or uncertainty exists when whether a given result or objective can be achieved—or how to achieve it—is not known or determined on the basis of generally available scientific or technological knowledge or experience, and cannot be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures (techniques, procedures, and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the field). Even where individual components are known, combining them in an unproven system configuration can generate genuine system-level technological uncertainty; consequently, courts and CRA auditors must evaluate a project holistically rather than improperly dissecting it into isolated component activities.

Shortly thereafter, in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 5087, 235 N.R. 258, [1998] F.C.J. No. 1590 (FCA, Docket A-710-96, December 21, 1998), the Federal Court of Appeal endorsed Justice Bowman's Northwest Hydraulic criteria at paragraph 10 and reversed a Tax Court decision that had denied an SR&ED claim for a concrete-forming medium despite finding that testing had produced a technological advance. The Federal Court of Appeal established a critical evidentiary rule:

"Once the Tax Court Judge had found that testing had taken place resulting in a technological advance, he erred in imposing the additional evidentiary burden of having to adduce documentary evidence relating to the repeatability of the testing data. Having reached the conclusion that a technological advance had taken place, there was a rebuttable inference that the testing in issue had been carried out in accordance with the SRED criteria in Regulation 2900."

Following RIS-Christie, the CRA's Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors explicitly instructs RTAs that they must not state that a technological advancement occurred while simultaneously disallowing a claim due to a lack of supporting evidence; instead, if evidence is inadequate, the RTA must state that the claimed work is unsubstantiated and that no eligibility determination is given.

In C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393, [2002] 1 C.T.C. 212 (FCA), at paragraph 17, the Federal Court of Appeal summarized Justice Bowman's Northwest Hydraulic criteria into the canonical Five-Question Test:

items: Was there a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures?
Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty?
Did the procedure adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses?
Did the process result in a technological advancement?
Was a detailed record of the hypotheses tested, and results kept as the work progressed?

body.text: 6.2 Strict Adherence to the Scientific Method and Personnel Qualifications: Kam-Press, Jentel, and Joel Theatrical Rigging

Taxpayers have periodically challenged the third Northwest Hydraulic criterion by arguing that the phrase "scientific method" does not appear verbatim in the text of subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. In Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen, 2021 FCA 88 (Docket A-442-19)—reaffirming its earlier appellate holdings in Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, 2011 FCA 355 and R&D Pro-Innovation Inc. v. Canada, 2016 FCA 152—the Federal Court of Appeal (per Justice Webb) rejected this argument and dismissed the taxpayer's appeal with costs. The Federal Court of Appeal held that in setting out the five criteria in Northwest Hydraulic, Justice Bowman was interpreting the statutory definition of SR&ED, and that a taxpayer must satisfy all five criteria, including adherence to the scientific method and proving genuine technological risk and advancement.

The practical boundary between systematic scientific investigation and ineligible "trial and error" was further delineated in Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6. In that case, the taxpayer sought to develop a motorized device activating a hydraulic system to control the descent rate of a theatre fire curtain (replacing conventional counterweights). The Tax Court of Canada dismissed the appeal and upheld the CRA's refusal on three grounds. First, regarding the qualifications of the research team, none of the internal employees held a university degree in engineering or a technical diploma in mechanical or hydraulic design, no specialized external resources were engaged, and no witnesses with engineering training were called. Because "routine engineering" is measured against techniques accessible to competent professionals in the field, a team lacking baseline engineering qualifications could not establish that the problems encountered exceeded routine engineering. Second, defining a hypothesis as "a statement to be tested by an experiment or a trial", the Court found that the taxpayer failed to formulate specific hypotheses prior to testing. Third, the experimental process lacked quantitative rigour: during its trials, the taxpayer never precisely measured the weights used or the duration of the fire curtain's descent from one trial to the next. (Similarly, in Mac & Mac Hydrodemolition Services Inc. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC, Justice Graham ruled against the taxpayer where supporting evidence failed to demonstrate adherence to the five questions45.)
6.3 Economic & Business Constraints vs. Pure Cost Targets: National R&D Inc. and 6398316 Canada Inc.

A frequent audit issue in commercial experimental development is whether cost, price, or economic constraints can give rise to technological uncertainty. Two Tax Court of Canada decisions define the legal boundary. In National R&D Inc. v. The Queen, 2020 TCC 47—which involved the development of a computer program to automate portions of filing SR&ED claims—Justice Lafleur held at paragraph 44 that "economic considerations" can impose uncertainty on a project, and that "[b]usiness constraints and the business context of the taxpayer that is claiming the SR&ED deduction and credit are relevant factors to take into account when considering the criterion of technological uncertainty".

By contrast, in 6398316 Canada Inc. v. The Queen, 2021 TCC 17, the taxpayer designed and constructed an energy-efficient house requiring no grid-tied fuel for heating and cooling by harnessing environmental temperature fluctuations, and framed its technological uncertainty as whether it could construct such a furnace-free house at a price point comparable to a traditional house. Justice Russell dismissed the appeal, holding that "[c]onceptually there is no technological aspect implicit in the notion of an item costing or priced at 'x' rather than 'y' dollars". Formulating technological uncertainty solely as a matter of cost "misses [the] Northwest Hydraulic target". Synthesizing National R&D Inc. and 6398316 Canada Inc. alongside the CRA's 2021 Guidelines on the eligibility of work, cost efficiency in and of itself is never a technological uncertainty; however, when economic or cost targets act as interlocking constraints that force engineers to attempt to achieve physical or system performance using novel architectures or constrained materials—creating genuine technological uncertainty—the project qualifies, provided the hypothesis is framed around the technological obstacle rather than the financial price point.
6.4 Contemporaneous Documentation, Failed Formulations, and Oral Testimony: Canafric Inc. v. The King (2023 TCC)

In Canafric Inc. v. The King (2023 TCC), the Tax Court of Canada delivered a significant taxpayer victory clarifying how the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria apply to incremental product development and gaps in written records. Canafric Inc., a food manufacturer developing custom frozen pie recipes for major retailers (such as Costco, Loblaws, and Mortimer), appealed the CRA's denial of SR&ED projects across its 2013 to 2016 taxation years ($343,449 in denied expenditures and $60,963 in denied ITCs, excluding 2014 figures).

The Tax Court of Canada allowed Canafric's appeal in full. On Questions 1 and 4 (The "Why" Requirement), Canafric established that no publicly available food-science information showed how to simultaneously achieve conflicting client targets—such as longer shelf life (21 days without preservatives), lower salt and fat, higher protein, maintaining product and pie crust integrity post-freezing, using real potatoes and antibiotic-free halal meat, thicker fillings, and shorter cooking times—and the Court held that eliminating failed recipe formulations constituted a valid technological advancement even when not every target was met. On Questions 2 and 3 (The "How" Requirement), the Court rejected the CRA's allegation of routine "trial and error," finding that Canafric systematically analyzed why specific recipes failed during testing and taste-panel evaluations and modified its hypotheses accordingly. Finally, on Question 5 (Documentation), citing RIS-Christie, the Court held that contemporaneous written documentation is not strictly mandatory where detailed, factually grounded oral testimony (provided by Canafric's CEO, Mr. Pandya, during CRA site visits and in court) credibly fills gaps in the documentary record.
